item.title: Fragility of Aeolian Ripples
item.description: arXiv:2611.14739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sand surfaces exposed to the wind are covered by aeolian sand waves of diverse wavelengths, from centimetres for small ripples to decameters for dunes. Sand dunes can be said to be antifragile, since their growth is not prohibited by storms, whereas ripples and megaripples are fragile since they get flattened. The fluid-entrainment hypothesis attributes their fragility to a common cause: the spontaneous aerodynamic entrainment of grains. Here, we challenge this conventional view by revealing its major shortcomings and inconsistencies. An alternative framework, routed in the granular bed rheology, posits that impact ripples are erased when the two-phase flow of ballistically hopping grains on a solid sand surface gives way to a three-phase flow, featuring an intermediate, collision-dominated, fluid-like transport layer. Notably, both martian wind-drag ripples and terrestrial aerodynamic ripples, which emerge via a hydrodynamic instability, are insensitive to such "surface-melting". Their destruction is predicated on the transition from aerodynamically smooth to rough conditions, instead. Our theoretical arguments are well supported by a stability diagram in terms of Shields number and grain diameter, assembled from a carefully reassessed large body of literature, and backed up by dedicated control measurements.
item.dc:creator: Constantin Rein, Katharina Tholen, Lior Saban, Itzhak Katra, Hezi Yizhaq, Klaus Kroy

item.title: Data-driven Reconstruction of the Phase Dynamics for the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation Reveals Seasonality and Statistical Synchronization with the Annual Cycle
item.description: arXiv:2611.14868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, we treat the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) as a rhythmic system periodically forced by the annual cycle. We examine ENSO event seasonality and synchronization between the annual and ENSO cycles. We compute phase time series for both cycles from sea surface temperature data using a data-driven Koopman operator approach. We then use Bayesian inference to reconstruct phase equations describing how the phases of the two oscillators evolve. The reconstructed two-variable phase equations show that the annual cycle modulates the instantaneous frequency of the fundamental ENSO mode. Stochastic simulations of these equations incorporating the estimated stationary noise indicate that El Ni\~{n}o and La Ni\~{n}a events tend to last longer when they start in boreal summer and that the variability of their durations is greater when they start in boreal spring. Furthermore, the averaged form of the phase equations indicates statistical $3:1$ phase locking between the annual and ENSO cycles, whereas no statistical phase locking is found for the other $m:n$ ratios.
item.dc:creator: Takahiro Arai, Yoji Kawamura

item.title: Advancing global water cycle science with the upcoming MAGIC satellite mission through data assimilation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The GRACE and GRACE-FO missions provide unique global measurements of terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA) from space since 2003. However, in order to spatially downscale the GRACE/-FO resolution of 300 km further, and to vertically disaggregate TWSA into soil moisture, groundwater and other contributions, the TWSA observations were assimilated into hydrological and land surface models in the past while improving the realism of the models. With the upcoming MAGIC (Mass Change and Geosciences International Constellation) constellation consisting of two satellite pairs (NASA/DLR GRACE-C and ESA NGGM), significant advancements are expected for the monitoring of water mass changes, with improved temporal and spatial resolution, reduced latency, and with lower noise levels. In this study, we reviewed the capabilities and limitations of existing GRACE/-FO data assimilation systems. We then investigated the benefit of including data from the upcoming MAGIC constellation into existing assimilation frameworks to improve not only data sets for water and carbon cycle science but also in view of operational applications, within a closed-loop simulation. For example, we extended a global 17 years GRACE/-FO assimilation era to a long time series of 33 years with synthetic MAGIC data assimilated and show reductions in groundwater trends errors and errors in identifying hydrological extreme events. We further showed for Europe that both storage and river runoff simulations benefit from more frequent assimilation, which the integration of MAGIC data will enable due to the foreseen 5-daily (instead of monthly) TWSA product. Finally, we demonstrated for the Iberian Peninsula and for Eastern Europe that MAGIC TWSA data assimilation also improved simulated carbon cycle variables via coupling in the land surface model, especially in water-limited regions.
item.dc:creator: Helena Gerdener, Yorck Ewerdwalbesloh, Anne Springer, Annika Nitschke, J\"urgen Kusche

item.title: Resolving Radiogenic Heterogeneity in the Earth's Mantle with Multi-Site Geo-neutrino Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2611.16715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a global fit to geo-neutrino measurements at four underground sites (Kamioka, Gran Sasso, Sudbury, Jiangmen), combining signal rates with site-specific predictions of the lithospheric contribution to constrain the quantity and distribution of radioactivity in the Earth's mantle. Assuming a uniform distribution of radioactivity in the mantle, we find a geo-neutrino rate of $S_\text{mantle} = 14.8 \pm 4.5$ NIU when the lithospheric predictions are allowed to vary within their uncertainties. This uniform mantle signal rate corresponds to radiogenic heating of $18.5 \pm 5.6$ TW. Although the uniform-mantle signal is resolved at $\sim3.2\sigma$, there is noticeable tension between the inferred mantle signals at Jiangmen and Kamioka, which may indicate non-uniform geo-neutrino production in the mantle. We explore six families of models to describe the heterogeneous spatial distribution of radiogenic elements in the Earth's mantle. Each model contains anomalous bodies or reservoirs carrying an excess of heat-producing elements over a depleted mantle (DM) background, with total inventory set by bulk-silicate-Earth mass balance and by a geochemical Th/U constraint. For each model, we compute the geo-response at each detector site and fit the resulting signals to the four measurements. A total of 968,274 individual model configurations are defined and tested. The results of $\sim$3 million distinct fits show that no plausible mantle or lithosphere model applied uniformly to all four sites reproduces the difference between the inferred mantle signals at the Jiangmen and Kamioka sites. Only local, site-specific prescriptions are able to reach the observed difference, suggesting that the Kamioka-Jiangmen tension is due to a local effect or statistical scatter, rather than large-scale mantle structure.
item.dc:creator: Michael Leyton, Stephen T. Dye

item.title: A Transferable Pretrained 3D Model for Impedance Inversion with Sparse-Well Prior Conditioning
item.description: arXiv:2611.14922v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep-learning-based seismic impedance inversion commonly requires retraining for each target survey, which may generalize poorly beyond the conditioning locations when well control is extremely sparse. We propose a transferable three-dimensional inversion framework that separates offline learning from target-survey deployment. A masked autoencoder first learns seismic structural representations from unlabeled multi-survey data, after which the frozen encoder is incorporated into an inversion network trained on synthetic geological models with sparse-well-derived low-frequency priors. During deployment, the complete inversion network remains fixed; the available conditioning well is used only to construct the low-frequency prior and align the global impedance range. Experiments on the Overthrust model show that the proposed method achieves the lowest full-volume NRMSE and reduces the P95 trace-wise NRMSE from 0.1310 to 0.1074 relative to the best target-trained baseline, indicating fewer localized large errors under different well locations. In a field survey with one conditioning well and three blind wells, it reduces the mean blind-well NRMSE by 20.95% relative to the target-trained U-Net while maintaining the highest correlation. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework transfers useful impedance information beyond the conditioning location with low deployment cost and without retraining the inversion network.
item.dc:creator: Gen Li, Zhaoyun Zong, Diqiong Jiang, Man Tang

item.title: A Diffusive T-Matrix Unifying the Electric and Magnetic Polarizability Tensors in Conducting Layered Media
item.description: arXiv:2611.15090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electromagnetic induction is used to detect and classify buried and submerged objects, such as unexploded ordnance in soil and on the seabed. A small object is commonly described by its magnetic polarizability tensor (MPT), which is independent of its position and of the sensor. The MPT assumes that the surrounding medium does not conduct. In seawater at extremely low frequency, or in clay at kilohertz frequencies, this assumption fails at depths comparable to the skin depth. The object then also diverts the current induced in the medium, a galvanic response that the MPT omits. We describe the object instead by its transition matrix (T-matrix), which keeps the independence from position and sensor and includes both responses. It is computed once per medium and frequency from a single finite element problem, for any shape and materials. Its inductive block reduces to the MPT when the medium conducts weakly, and its galvanic block reduces to the electric polarizability tensor in the static limit. We test the model against full finite element solutions for a conducting box, non-magnetic and permeable, in a layered sea and in clay over bedrock. Two orders beyond the dipole, it is accurate to within 1.4% over two decades of frequency and for sizes up to 0.7 of the depth, whereas the error of the MPT carried into the conducting medium reaches 91%. Blocks coupling the two responses, contained in neither tensor, contribute up to 13%.
item.dc:creator: Fraser Williams, Dhammika Jayalath, Clinton Fookes, Ajay Pandey

item.title: Imputing Missing Near-Surface Air Temperature using Graph Attention Networks with Distance-Aware Edge Features
item.description: arXiv:2611.15598v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a graph attention network for reconstructing near-surface air temperature fields from incomplete observations. The model represents each grid cell as a node connected to its $k$ nearest neighbors, with attention weights that depend on node features, distance, and land-ocean transitions. This graph representation avoids the polar distortions associated with treating the globe as a flat latitude-longitude image, as most deep learning reconstruction methods do. This is particularly relevant for historical temperature records, which extend back to the mid-nineteenth century but remain incomplete, with the largest gaps early in the record and at high latitudes. We train our model on CMIP6 CESM2 historical simulations masked with the time-varying HadCRUT5 observational coverage from 1850 to 2014. We then compare our approach with ordinary kriging, GraphEM, and the LaMa inpainting network on a held-out realization. The graph model achieves the lowest spatial RMSE (0.997 K), 10.1% lower than LaMa and approximately 31% lower than kriging and GraphEM. The largest gains occur in the Arctic and Antarctic, while LaMa remains slightly more accurate in the densely observed tropics. The graph model's error also falls faster as coverage increases, so its advantage over LaMa grows by more than a third from the 1850s to the 2000s. An ablation study shows that the model's skill comes mainly from the geometric graph construction rather than from auxiliary physical covariates.
item.dc:creator: Emma C. Weber, Dominique Guillot, Daniyar Abykhanov, Julien Emile-Geay

item.title: Constructive Reuse of Free-Surface Ghost Wavefields in Marine Seismic Data: A Propagation-Based Framework
item.description: arXiv:2602.07759v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in marine seismic acquisition and processing have substantially improved the decomposition of free surface ghost wavefields. Building upon these developments, this study proposes a propagation-based framework in which decomposed ghost wavefields are treated as physically meaningful components that can be constructively reused as additional wavefield components. Starting from a finite inverse expansion of the ghost operator, a recursive formulation is derived and implemented through adaptive predictive decomposition. The formulation is subsequently extended to multidimensional wavefields through wavefield extrapolation and reciprocity, enabling decomposition into components associated with real and mirrored sources and receivers. The decomposed wavefields are then restored to a common acquisition geometry by survey sinking and combined through wavefield superposition, forming a preprocessing module that can be incorporated into conventional marine seismic processing workflows. Synthetic examples demonstrate increased signal strength through ghost reuse, spectral amplitude recovery of ghost-related notches including frequencies near DC, and clear decomposition of ghost-related wavefield components. Field-data examples acquired using a conventional shallow-towed airgun survey further demonstrate improvements in reflector continuity and coherent reflection energy, together with partial restoration of spectral amplitudes degraded by the free surface ghost, supporting the practical applicability of the proposed framework. The proposed framework therefore provides a processing-based complement to conventional ghost decomposition technologies and suggests a unified approach in which acquisition geometry and ghost processing are jointly optimised to maximise the usable wavefield information.
item.dc:creator: Hitoshi Mikada

item.title: Field-Deployable Hybrid Gravimetry: Projecting Absolute Accuracy Across a Remote 24km$^2$ Survey via Daily Quantum Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2602.10557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hybrid gravimetry combines the mobility of relative gravimeters with the long-term stability of an absolute reference. Following our previous demonstration of this concept under controlled field conditions (Shettell et al., 2024), we investigate whether quantum-assisted hybrid gravimetry retains its calibration performance during an extended survey under realistic operational constraints. A transportable atomic gravimeter provided routine $\mu$Gal-level calibration of two mobile spring gravimeters throughout a seven-day survey spanning 24 km$^2$ of dense tropical terrain. Despite rainfall, dense canopy, and limited field infrastructure, the atomic reference enabled high-precision asynchronous comparison of relative measurements while suppressing instrumental drift in regions where GPS positioning remained reliable. These results demonstrate that transportable atomic gravimeters can provide practical calibration references for extended geophysical surveys, extending hybrid quantum gravimetry beyond controlled demonstrations toward realistic field deployment.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Shettell, Kai Sheng Lee, Fong En Oon, Elizaveta Maksimova, Hong Hui Chen, Rainer Dumke

item.title: Automatic Knowledge Graph Construction and Query for Earthquake Catalogs
item.description: arXiv:2607.24984v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent years, the number of events in earthquake catalogs has significantly increased due to the utilization of more effective deep learning based detectors and phase pickers but answering open ended questions such as what characterizes this sequence? remains constrained by rigid spatiotemporal windowing and subjective expert interpretation. We present the first systematic application of graph based retrieval augmented generation GraphRAG directly to raw, tabular catalog records across three independently featured catalogs, a reservoir adjacent swarm, the 2019 Ridgecrest tectonic sequence, and the 2021 Maduo Mw7.4 aftershock sequence. Without the need for manual data structuring, the pipeline builds structurally complete, queryable knowledge graphs for all three. Rigorous evaluation individually verified against catalog derived ground truth and a rule based reference graph exposes failure modes, and four seismology informed prompt fixes eliminate all targeted fabrications while sharply improving mechanism reasoning. A vector RAG baseline demonstrates the graph layers distinctive value, catalog wide summarization and temporal stage comparison. In addition, we have identified two main pitfalls that need attention. GraphRAG thus offers a practical, transferable, near zero cost query interface for earthquake catalogs, where careful prompting ensures the results are consistently accurate and trustworthy.
item.dc:creator: Yuxin Zhou, Huai Zhang, S. Mostafa Mousavi

item.title: Tidal potential measured with distant optical clocks
item.description: arXiv:2611.14293v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fibre-linked optical clocks sense tidal changes of the gravitational potential, but separating overlapping tidal components and quantifying their precision remain challenging. Using strontium and ytterbium clocks 692 km apart, we measure over 353 days a response of 0.95 (0.11) to the combined solid-Earth and ocean-loading tide and 1.01 (0.13) for the lunar semidiurnal group, and separate the lunar and solar-frequency semidiurnal contributions. A signal-to-noise model based on the actual sampling accounts for the lunar precision and guides future clock-network observations.
